paragraphs.text: Glucose phosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency is an autosomal recessive cause of congenital nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia. Patients have chronic hemolysis, with hemolytic crises during acute infections, and splenectomy can improve the anemia (Arnold, 1979; Shalev et al., 1993). Some patients also have neurologic involvement, such as mental retardation, myopathy, or muscular hypotonia (Zanella et al., 1980; Schroter et al., 1985; Kugler et al., 1998).

paragraphs.text: Hutton and Chilcote (1974) observed 8 children (5 living and 3 deceased) from 2 families in Kentucky and Indiana with severe hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia caused by GPI deficiency. All affected children were severely anemic early in life. The 3 deaths occurred in young patients who did not receive adequate blood transfusions or whose parents refused to permit splenectomy. Splenectomy generally removed the need for blood transfusion, and no patient needed regular transfusion after puberty. Growth and development were surprisingly normal, and no patient died of infection.

paragraphs.text: Rotteveel et al. (1977) reported a Dutch patient with GPI deficiency type Nijmegen. The patient had nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia that presented in the neonatal period. The degree of hemolysis stayed the same over the years, but trivial infections often triggered increased hemolysis that required blood transfusion. The patient was doubly heterozygous for 2 different GPI-deficient alleles. Parents and grandparents carrying one of these alleles showed no sign of hemolysis, including no shortened red cell survival.

paragraphs.text: Kugler et al. (1998) found compound heterozygosity for a 59A-C transversion in the GPI gene, resulting in a his20-to-pro (H20P) substitution, and a 1016T-C transition, resulting in a leu339-to-pro (L339P) substitution, in the patient with GPI Homburg. That patient had congenital hemolytic anemia with myopathy and mental retardation (Schroter et al., 1985). Kugler et al. (1998) considered that the inserted proline was likely to affect enzyme folding and activity.

checks.claim: The patient with GPI Homburg had congenital hemolytic anemia with myopathy and mental retardation.

checks.explanation: The abstract states all three features directly.

checks.evidence_quote: Owing to the insertion of proline, the H20P and L339P mutations are likely to affect the folding and activity of the enzyme.

paragraphs.text: Kugler et al. (1998) studied 2 sibs with severe GPI deficiency (GPI Calden) and no neurologic symptoms. They identified 2 mutations in the GPI gene: a 1166A-G transition, resulting in a his389-to-arg (H389R) substitution, and a 1549C-G transversion, resulting in a leu517-to-val (L517V) substitution. Both changes are located at the subunit interface.
